1	# Leveraging Standout: Value and Implementation Quality Checklist
2	
3	Standout is most valuable when it creates a testable seam between application
4	behavior and shell presentation. Use this guide to review an implementation,
5	decide which framework capabilities add value, and name missing framework
6	support without pushing presentation concerns back into handlers.
7	
8	## Evaluation classes
9	
10	Classify every finding before deciding whether it needs work:
11	
12	- **Invariant** — a property the application should preserve wherever Standout
13	  owns a command. Violating it weakens the architecture or public behavior.
14	- **Applicable capability** — a Standout feature that is valuable only when the
15	  application's needs call for it. Not using it is not automatically a defect.
16	- **Framework gap** — a desirable behavior that Standout does not currently
17	  integrate. Record the gap instead of hiding a custom workaround in a handler.
18	
19	The checklist uses **I**, **A**, and **G** for those classes.
20	
21	## Ownership and dispatch
22	
23	- **I — Keep reusable behavior CLI-free.** Domain rules, state transitions,
24	  validation, persistence, and reusable services should expose ordinary Rust
25	  interfaces. A separate core crate is the recommended production shape, not a
26	  requirement enforced by Standout. Small applications may keep the same seam
27	  inside one crate.
28	- **I — Let the binary own the shell.** Clap types, Standout app construction,
29	  handlers, CLI view DTOs, templates, styles, environment lookup, and final
30	  output belong in the CLI package. Handlers are adapters: translate parsed
31	  arguments, call the core, and return serializable data.
32	- **I — Integrate with Clap.** Standout does not replace Clap. Clap remains the
33	  command and argument parser; Standout adds dispatch, rendering, output modes,
34	  hooks, and test seams around the resulting command model.
35	- **A — Prefer declarative dispatch when conventions fit.**
36	  `#[derive(Dispatch)]` maps Clap variants to handlers and can attach templates,
37	  hooks, nested dispatch, and pipes. Use explicit `command_with` registration
38	  when a command needs configuration that is clearer in builder code.
39	
40	The production-shaped [`todo-core` + `tdoo` example](production-shaped-example.md)
41	shows this ownership boundary in executable code. The
42	[dispatch guide](../crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md) covers the
43	pipeline in detail.
44	
45	## Output and rendering
46	
47	- **I — Return data, not presentation.** A normal handler returns
48	  `Output::Render(data)`, `Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`. It
49	  should not print, emit ANSI, render a template, or branch on output mode.
50	- **I — Let the framework own the write for reported artifacts.** When a command
51	  produces a file *and* a report, return `Output::Artifact(...)` with owned bytes,
52	  an opt-in suggested destination, and the report. Standout selects the
53	  destination, writes, and renders the report afterwards with a receipt — the
54	  application never opens the file or words a success it hasn't earned.
55	- **I — Keep one data contract across modes.** `auto`, `term`, and `text` render
56	  the MiniJinja template and transform semantic style tags. `term-debug` keeps
57	  the tags visible. Structured `json`, `yaml`, `xml`, and `csv` modes serialize
58	  handler data directly and bypass templates, including template-injected
59	  context.
60	- **A — Use MiniJinja and semantic CSS.** Put layout in file-backed MiniJinja
61	  templates and appearance in CSS classes such as `.title` or `.warning`.
62	  Define adaptive overrides with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` and
63	  `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`; Standout resolves the matching style
64	  variant for the terminal background.
65	- **A — Embed resources and keep the debug loop short.** `embed_templates!` and
66	  `embed_styles!` provide release-safe assets. Hot reload specifically means
67	  that debug file-backed resources are re-read on render, so source edits can
68	  be observed without rebuilding while the original paths remain available.
69	- **A — Use tabular layout for column relationships.** Reach for the `col`
70	  filter and tabular specifications when alignment, width allocation,
71	  truncation, or nested columns matter; do not hand-pad strings in handlers.
72	- **I — Use the right render diagnostic.** `--output term-debug` shows where
73	  style tags were placed, but it preserves known and unknown tags alike and
74	  does not validate that the tags exist. Use `validate_template` in development
75	  or tests to detect missing style definitions. Terminal mode's `?` marker is a
76	  visible warning, not a substitute for validation.
77	- **G — Do not imply integrated per-command CSV projection.** Normal app
78	  dispatch automatically flattens serializable data for CSV. The direct
79	  `render_auto_with_spec` API can render CSV with a `FlatDataSpec`, but arbitrary
80	  per-command projection through normal `App` dispatch is not currently
81	  integrated. Prefer a stable CLI-owned view DTO, or record the missing app
82	  configuration seam.
83	
84	See [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md),
85	[Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md),
86	[Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md),
87	[File System Resources](../crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md), and
88	[Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for the
89	focused APIs and trade-offs.
90	
91	## Testing pyramid
92	
93	- **I — Core tests:** exercise validation, filtering, state transitions, and
94	  persistence through the CLI-free Rust interface.
95	- **I — Adapter tests:** call the typed handler function directly and assert the
96	  CLI-to-core mapping plus returned view DTO.
97	- **I — Pipeline tests:** use `standout-test::TestHarness` for Clap parsing,
98	  dispatch, hooks, inputs, templates, structured modes, and controlled process
99	  seams. Mark harness tests serial because those seams are process-global.
100	- **A — Process tests:** reserve a small end-to-end layer for real PTYs,
101	  signals, subprocess behavior, and build or link boundaries the harness cannot
102	  model.
103	
104	This ordering keeps most failures close to their owner while still proving the
105	user-visible shell contract. See [Testing](../topics/testing.md) for the full
106	boundary matrix.
107	
108	## Optional application capabilities
109	
110	These are **applicable capabilities**, not baseline requirements:
111	
112	- **Hooks** place cross-command validation, request-context injection,
113	  serialized-data transformation, or post-output observation at an explicit
114	  pipeline phase.
115	- **Declarative input chains** resolve values from arguments, environment,
116	  stdin, clipboard, defaults, editors, or prompts with one validation path.
117	- **Pipes** send or transform rendered text after output; binary and silent
118	  results pass through unchanged.
119	- **Partial adoption** lets an existing Clap application delegate selected
120	  commands to Standout and retain its legacy path for unmatched commands.
121	
122	Adopt each capability only when it removes application-owned orchestration or
123	improves a test seam. If the framework cannot express the required behavior,
124	classify it as a framework gap and keep the workaround isolated in the CLI
125	layer.
126	
127	## Review outcome
128	
129	A high-quality implementation has no unresolved invariant violations, uses the
130	applicable capabilities that materially simplify its shell boundary, and names
131	framework gaps explicitly. That is a stronger signal than counting how many
132	Standout features an application uses.
133

# Leveraging Standout: Value and Implementation Quality Checklist

Standout is most valuable when it creates a testable seam between application
behavior and shell presentation. Use this guide to review an implementation,
decide which framework capabilities add value, and name missing framework
support without pushing presentation concerns back into handlers.

## Evaluation classes

Classify every finding before deciding whether it needs work:

- **Invariant** — a property the application should preserve wherever Standout
  owns a command. Violating it weakens the architecture or public behavior.
- **Applicable capability** — a Standout feature that is valuable only when the
  application's needs call for it. Not using it is not automatically a defect.
- **Framework gap** — a desirable behavior that Standout does not currently
  integrate. Record the gap instead of hiding a custom workaround in a handler.

The checklist uses **I**, **A**, and **G** for those classes.

## Ownership and dispatch

- **I — Keep reusable behavior CLI-free.** Domain rules, state transitions,
  validation, persistence, and reusable services should expose ordinary Rust
  interfaces. A separate core crate is the recommended production shape, not a
  requirement enforced by Standout. Small applications may keep the same seam
  inside one crate.
- **I — Let the binary own the shell.** Clap types, Standout app construction,
  handlers, CLI view DTOs, templates, styles, environment lookup, and final
  output belong in the CLI package. Handlers are adapters: translate parsed
  arguments, call the core, and return serializable data.
- **I — Integrate with Clap.** Standout does not replace Clap. Clap remains the
  command and argument parser; Standout adds dispatch, rendering, output modes,
  hooks, and test seams around the resulting command model.
- **A — Prefer declarative dispatch when conventions fit.**
  `#[derive(Dispatch)]` maps Clap variants to handlers and can attach templates,
  hooks, nested dispatch, and pipes. Use explicit `command_with` registration
  when a command needs configuration that is clearer in builder code.

The production-shaped [`todo-core` + `tdoo` example](production-shaped-example.md)
shows this ownership boundary in executable code. The
[dispatch guide](../crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md) covers the
pipeline in detail.

## Output and rendering

- **I — Return data, not presentation.** A normal handler returns
  `Output::Render(data)`, `Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`. It
  should not print, emit ANSI, render a template, or branch on output mode.
- **I — Let the framework own the write for reported artifacts.** When a command
  produces a file *and* a report, return `Output::Artifact(...)` with owned bytes,
  an opt-in suggested destination, and the report. Standout selects the
  destination, writes, and renders the report afterwards with a receipt — the
  application never opens the file or words a success it hasn't earned.
- **I — Keep one data contract across modes.** `auto`, `term`, and `text` render
  the MiniJinja template and transform semantic style tags. `term-debug` keeps
  the tags visible. Structured `json`, `yaml`, `xml`, and `csv` modes serialize
  handler data directly and bypass templates, including template-injected
  context.
- **A — Use MiniJinja and semantic CSS.** Put layout in file-backed MiniJinja
  templates and appearance in CSS classes such as `.title` or `.warning`.
  Define adaptive overrides with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` and
  `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`; Standout resolves the matching style
  variant for the terminal background.
- **A — Embed resources and keep the debug loop short.** `embed_templates!` and
  `embed_styles!` provide release-safe assets. Hot reload specifically means
  that debug file-backed resources are re-read on render, so source edits can
  be observed without rebuilding while the original paths remain available.
- **A — Use tabular layout for column relationships.** Reach for the `col`
  filter and tabular specifications when alignment, width allocation,
  truncation, or nested columns matter; do not hand-pad strings in handlers.
- **I — Use the right render diagnostic.** `--output term-debug` shows where
  style tags were placed, but it preserves known and unknown tags alike and
  does not validate that the tags exist. Use `validate_template` in development
  or tests to detect missing style definitions. Terminal mode's `?` marker is a
  visible warning, not a substitute for validation.
- **G — Do not imply integrated per-command CSV projection.** Normal app
  dispatch automatically flattens serializable data for CSV. The direct
  `render_auto_with_spec` API can render CSV with a `FlatDataSpec`, but arbitrary
  per-command projection through normal `App` dispatch is not currently
  integrated. Prefer a stable CLI-owned view DTO, or record the missing app
  configuration seam.

See [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md),
[Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md),
[Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md),
[File System Resources](../crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md), and
[Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for the
focused APIs and trade-offs.

## Testing pyramid

- **I — Core tests:** exercise validation, filtering, state transitions, and
  persistence through the CLI-free Rust interface.
- **I — Adapter tests:** call the typed handler function directly and assert the
  CLI-to-core mapping plus returned view DTO.
- **I — Pipeline tests:** use `standout-test::TestHarness` for Clap parsing,
  dispatch, hooks, inputs, templates, structured modes, and controlled process
  seams. Mark harness tests serial because those seams are process-global.
- **A — Process tests:** reserve a small end-to-end layer for real PTYs,
  signals, subprocess behavior, and build or link boundaries the harness cannot
  model.

This ordering keeps most failures close to their owner while still proving the
user-visible shell contract. See [Testing](../topics/testing.md) for the full
boundary matrix.

## Optional application capabilities

These are **applicable capabilities**, not baseline requirements:

- **Hooks** place cross-command validation, request-context injection,
  serialized-data transformation, or post-output observation at an explicit
  pipeline phase.
- **Declarative input chains** resolve values from arguments, environment,
  stdin, clipboard, defaults, editors, or prompts with one validation path.
- **Pipes** send or transform rendered text after output; binary and silent
  results pass through unchanged.
- **Partial adoption** lets an existing Clap application delegate selected
  commands to Standout and retain its legacy path for unmatched commands.

Adopt each capability only when it removes application-owned orchestration or
improves a test seam. If the framework cannot express the required behavior,
classify it as a framework gap and keep the workaround isolated in the CLI
layer.

## Review outcome

A high-quality implementation has no unresolved invariant violations, uses the
applicable capabilities that materially simplify its shell boundary, and names
framework gaps explicitly. That is a stronger signal than counting how many
Standout features an application uses.

1	# File System Resources
2	
3	`standout-render` supports file-based templates and stylesheets that can be hot-reloaded during development and embedded into release binaries. This workflow combines the rapid iteration of interpreted languages with the distribution simplicity of compiled binaries.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## The Development Workflow
8	
9	During development, you want to:
10	
11	1. Edit a template or stylesheet
12	2. Re-run your program
13	3. See changes immediately
14	
15	During release, you want:
16	
17	1. A single binary with no external dependencies
18	2. No file paths to manage
19	3. No risk of missing assets
20	
21	`standout-render` supports both modes with the same code.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Hot Reload
26	
27	In debug builds (`debug_assertions` enabled), file-based templates are re-read from disk on each render. This means:
28	
29	- Edit `templates/report.jinja` → re-run → see changes
30	- No recompilation needed
31	
32	```rust
33	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme};
34	
35	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
36	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
37	
38	// In debug: reads from disk each time
39	// In release: content was scanned once at registration
40	let output = renderer.render("report", &data)?;
41	```
42	
43	### How It Works
44	
45	`Renderer` tracks the source of each template name:
46	
47	- **Inline** (`add_template`) and **embedded** (`with_embedded`, `with_embedded_source`) content: always cached, never re-read.
48	- **File-based** (`add_template_dir`): path recorded; in debug builds the file is re-read before each render, so edits are visible without recompiling.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Supported Extensions
53	
54	### Templates
55	
56	| Extension | Priority |
57	| ----------- | ---------- |
58	| `.jinja` | 1 (highest) |
59	| `.jinja2` | 2 |
60	| `.j2` | 3 |
61	| `.stpl` | 4 |
62	| `.txt` | 5 (lowest) |
63	
64	If both `report.jinja` and `report.txt` exist in the same directory, `report.jinja` is used. A lookup tries the given name exactly first; if that carries one of the extensions above, it also tries the name with that extension stripped.
65	
66	### Stylesheets
67	
68	| Extension | Format |
69	| ----------- | -------- |
70	| `.css` | CSS syntax |
71	| `.yaml` | YAML syntax |
72	| `.yml` | YAML syntax |
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Embedding Resources
77	
78	For release builds, embed resources into the binary at compile time with `embed_templates!` / `embed_styles!`. Each macro reads matching files under the given directory and returns an `EmbeddedTemplates` / `EmbeddedStyles` value (both are `EmbeddedSource<R>`, differing only in the resource kind).
79	
80	```rust
81	use standout_render::{embed_templates, embed_styles, Renderer, Theme};
82	
83	let templates = embed_templates!("src/templates");
84	let styles = embed_styles!("src/styles");
85	
86	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
87	renderer.with_embedded_source(templates);
88	```
89	
90	`EmbeddedSource::should_hot_reload()` is `true` in debug builds when the original source directory (recorded at compile time) still exists on disk. What that buys depends on which consumer takes the value, and the two differ:
91	
92	- **`App::builder().templates(embedded)` / `.styles(embedded)`** call `EmbeddedSource::into_registry`, which under `should_hot_reload()` walks the source directory and registers the entries as **file-backed**. A debug build therefore re-reads them per render, exactly like `add_template_dir`. See the standout framework docs for that wiring.
93	- **`Renderer::with_embedded_source`** builds that registry and then copies every resolved entry in with `add_inline`. The content is **snapshotted at registration**, so a `Renderer` does not re-read the source directory afterwards — `should_hot_reload()` changes nothing a caller can observe on this path.
94	
95	### Hybrid Approach
96	
97	Combine embedded defaults with an optional file directory. The directory **adds** names; it cannot replace one, because tier 1 is consulted first (see [Resolution Priority](#resolution-priority)) and `with_embedded_source` has already put every embedded name there:
98	
99	```rust
100	use standout_render::{embed_templates, Renderer, Theme};
101	use std::path::Path;
102	
103	let embedded = embed_templates!("src/templates");
104	
105	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
106	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded);
107	
108	// Only reached for names not already resolved above
109	if Path::new("./templates").exists() {
110	    renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
111	}
112	```
113	
114	So `./templates` supplies templates the binary does not embed. A same-named file there is **not** an override: `render("report")` still resolves the embedded `report`. To let a directory win over the binary's copy, do not register the embedded source at all when the directory exists.
115	
116	---
117	
118	## Resolution Priority
119	
120	`Renderer` resolves a name in two tiers:
121	
122	1. **Inline and embedded** — `add_template` and `with_embedded`/`with_embedded_source` write into the same namespace. Whichever call registered a name last wins; there's no separate priority between "inline" and "embedded" content.
123	2. **File-based directories** (`add_template_dir`) — checked only for a name not already resolved in tier 1.
124	
125	Registering the **same name from two different directories is a collision error**, not a silent override — file-based names must be unique across every directory you register.
126	
127	```rust
128	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded);   // Tier 1
129	renderer.add_template("report", "inline"); // Tier 1 — overwrites "report" if embedded also defined it
130	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?; // Tier 2 — only used for names tier 1 doesn't have
131	```
132	
133	---
134	
135	## Directory Structure
136	
137	Recommended project layout:
138	
139	```text
140	my-cli/
141	├── src/
142	│   ├── main.rs
143	│   ├── templates/           # Templates for embedding
144	│   │   ├── list.jinja
145	│   │   ├── detail.jinja
146	│   │   └── partials/
147	│   │       └── header.jinja
148	│   └── styles/              # Stylesheets for embedding
149	│       ├── default.css
150	│       └── colorblind.css
151	├── templates/               # Extra development templates (gitignored)
152	└── styles/                  # Extra development stylesheets (gitignored)
153	```
154	
155	In `main.rs`:
156	
157	```rust
158	use std::path::Path;
159	
160	let embedded_templates = embed_templates!("src/templates");
161	
162	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
163	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded_templates);
164	
165	// In debug, also pick up local templates the binary does not embed.
166	// Names the binary already embeds keep resolving to the embedded copy.
167	#[cfg(debug_assertions)]
168	{
169	    if Path::new("./templates").exists() {
170	        renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
171	    }
172	}
173	```
174	
175	---
176	
177	## Error Handling
178	
179	### Missing Templates
180	
181	```rust
182	match renderer.render("nonexistent", &data) {
183	    Ok(output) => println!("{}", output),
184	    Err(e) => {
185	        // Template not found in any source
186	        eprintln!("Template error: {}", e);
187	    }
188	}
189	```
190	
191	### Name Collisions
192	
193	Same-directory collisions use extension priority (`.jinja` beats `.txt`, etc. — see the table above).
194	
195	Collisions across two different directories registered with `add_template_dir` are reported as `RegistryError::Collision`, not silently resolved by registration order.
196	
197	### Invalid Content
198	
199	Template syntax errors are reported with the template name and the underlying engine's message.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## API Reference
204	
205	### Renderer
206	
207	The primary entry point for most applications:
208	
209	```rust
210	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme};
211	
212	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
213	
214	// Templates
215	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
216	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
217	renderer.with_embedded_source(embed_templates!("src/templates"));
218	
219	// Render
220	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
221	let count = renderer.template_count();
222	```
223	
224	### TemplateRegistry
225	
226	The lower-level registry `Renderer` builds on internally. Use it directly only when bypassing `Renderer`:
227	
228	```rust
229	use standout_render::TemplateRegistry;
230	
231	let mut registry = TemplateRegistry::new();
232	
233	registry.add_inline("greeting", "Hello, {{ name }}!");
234	registry.add_embedded(embedded_map); // HashMap<String, String>
235	
236	// Query — `get` returns the resolved source, not the raw content
237	let resolved = registry.get("greeting")?;   // Result<ResolvedTemplate, RegistryError>
238	let content = registry.get_content("greeting")?; // Result<String, RegistryError>
239	let names: Vec<&str> = registry.names().collect();
240	```
241	
242	### StylesheetRegistry
243	
244	```rust
245	use standout_render::StylesheetRegistry;
246	
247	let mut registry = StylesheetRegistry::new();
248	registry.add_dir("./styles")?;
249	registry.add_embedded(embedded_themes); // HashMap<String, Theme>
250	
251	let theme = registry.get("default")?;      // Result<Theme, StylesheetError>
252	let exists: bool = registry.contains("default");
253	let names: Vec<&str> = registry.names().collect();
254	```
255	
256	### Embed Macros
257	
258	```rust
259	use standout_render::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
260	
261	// At compile time, reads all matching files and embeds their content
262	let templates = embed_templates!("path/to/templates");
263	let styles = embed_styles!("path/to/styles");
264	```
265

1	# Standout How To
2	
3	This is a small, focused guide for adopting Standout in a working shell application. Each step is self-sufficient, takes a positive step towards a sane CLI design, and can be incrementally merged. This can be done for one command (probably a good idea), then replicated to as many as you'd like.
4	
5	Note that only 2 out of 8 steps are Standout related. The others are generally good practices and clear designs for maintainable shell programs. This is not an accident, as Standout's goal is to allow your app to keep a great structure effortlessly, while providing testability, rich and fast output design, and more.
6	
7	For explanation's sake, we will show a hypothetical list command for tdoo, a todo list manager.
8	
9	This guide keeps the migration in one package so each step is small. Once the
10	application behavior is separated from output, move it into a CLI-free library;
11	the canonical [production-shaped application](production-shaped-example.md)
12	shows the final ownership model.
13	
14	**See Also:**
15	
16	- [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) - detailed handler API
17	- [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) - dependency injection patterns
18	- [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) - themes and styles in depth
19	- [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md) - all output format options
20	- [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) - migrating incrementally
21	- [Input Collection](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) - declarative input from multiple sources
22	
23	## 1. Start: The Argument Parsing
24	
25	Arg parsing is insanely intricate and deceptively simple. In case you are not already: define your application's interface with clap. Nothing else is worth doing until you have a sane starting point.
26	
27	If you don't have clap set up yet, here's a minimal starting point:
28	
29	```rust
30	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
31	
32	#[derive(Parser)]
33	#[command(name = "tdoo")]
34	struct Cli {
35	    #[command(subcommand)]
36	    command: Commands,
37	}
38	
39	#[derive(Subcommand)]
40	enum Commands {
41	    /// List all todos
42	    List {
43	        #[arg(short, long)]
44	        all: bool,
45	    },
46	    /// Add a new todo
47	    Add {
48	        title: String,
49	    },
50	}
51	
52	fn main() {
53	    let cli = Cli::parse();
54	    match cli.command {
55	        Commands::List { all } => list_command(all),
56	        Commands::Add { title } => add_command(&title),
57	    }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	(If you are using a non-clap-compatible crate, for now, you'd have to write an adapter for clap.)
62	
63	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
64	
65	## 2. Hard Split Logic and Formatting
66	
67	Now, your command should be split into two functions: the logic handler and its rendering. Don't worry about the specifics, do the straightest path from your current code.
68	
69	This is the one key step, the key design rule. And that's not because Standout requires it, rather the other way around: Standout is designed on top of it, and keeping it separate and easy to iterate on both logic and presentation under this design is Standout's key value.
70	
71	If your CLI is in good shape this will be a small task, otherwise you may find yourself patching together print statements everywhere, tidying up the data model and centralizing the processing. The silver lining here being: if it takes considerable work, there will be considerable gain in doing so.
72	
73	**Before** (tangled logic and output):
74	
75	```rust
76	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
77	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
78	    println!("Your Todos:");
79	    println!("-----------");
80	    for (i, todo) in todos.iter().enumerate() {
81	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
82	            let marker = if todo.status == Status::Done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" };
83	            println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, marker, todo.title);
84	        }
85	    }
86	    if todos.is_empty() {
87	        println!("No todos yet!");
88	    }
89	}
90	```
91	
92	**After** (clean separation):
93	
94	```rust
95	use clap::ArgMatches;
96	
97	// Data types for your domain
98	#[derive(Clone)]
99	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
100	
101	#[derive(Clone)]
102	pub struct Todo {
103	    pub title: String,
104	    pub status: Status,
105	}
106	
107	pub struct TodoResult {
108	    pub message: Option<String>,
109	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
110	}
111	
112	// This is your application function. It knows nothing about clap and returns
113	// an ordinary Rust data type.
114	//
115	// Note: This example uses immutable references. If your application service
116	// needs mutable state (&mut self), see the "Mutable Handlers" section below.
117	pub fn list(show_done: bool) -> TodoResult {
118	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
119	
120	    let filtered: Vec<Todo> = if show_done {
121	        todos
122	    } else {
123	        todos.into_iter()
124	            .filter(|t| matches!(t.status, Status::Pending))
125	            .collect()
126	    };
127	
128	    TodoResult {
129	        message: None,
130	        todos: filtered,
131	    }
132	}
133	
134	// This will take the Rust data type and print the result to stdout
135	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
136	    if let Some(msg) = result.message {
137	        println!("{}", msg);
138	    }
139	    for (i, todo) in result.todos.iter().enumerate() {
140	        let status = match todo.status {
141	            Status::Done => "[x]",
142	            Status::Pending => "[ ]",
143	        };
144	        println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, status, todo.title);
145	    }
146	}
147	
148	// And the orchestrator:
149	pub fn list_command(matches: &ArgMatches) {
150	    render_list(list(matches.get_flag("all")))
151	}
152	```
153	
154	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` and then `tdoo list` - output should look identical to before.
155	
156	### Intermezzo A: Milestone - Logic and Presentation Split
157	
158	**What you achieved:** Your command logic is now a pure function that returns data.
159	**What's now possible:**
160	
161	- All of your app's logic can be unit tested as any code, from the logic inwards.
162	- You can test by passing domain inputs directly to the application function.
163	- The rendering can also be tested by feeding data inputs and matching outputs (though this is brittle).
164	
165	**What's next:** Making the return type serializable for automatic JSON/YAML output.
166	**Your files now:**
167	
168	```text
169	src/
170	├── main.rs          # clap setup + orchestrators
171	├── core.rs          # list(), add() - CLI-free application behavior
172	└── render.rs        # render_list(), render_add() - output formatting
173	```
174	
175	## 3. Fine Tune the Application Result Type
176	
177	While any data type works, Standout's renderer takes a generic type that must implement `Serialize`. This enables automatic JSON/YAML output modes and template rendering through MiniJinja's context system. This is likely a small change, and beneficial as a baseline for logic results that will simplify writing renderers later.
178	
179	Add serde to your `Cargo.toml`:
180	
181	```toml
182	[dependencies]
183	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
184	```
185	
186	Update your types:
187	
188	```rust
189	use serde::Serialize;
190	
191	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
192	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
193	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
194	
195	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
196	pub struct Todo {
197	    pub title: String,
198	    pub status: Status,
199	}
200	
201	#[derive(Serialize)]
202	pub struct TodoResult {
203	    pub message: Option<String>,
204	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
205	}
206	```
207	
208	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
209	
210	## 4. Replace Imperative Print Statements With a Template
211	
212	Reading a template of an output next to the substituting variables is much easier to reason about than scattered prints, string concats and the like.
213	
214	This step is optional - if your current output is simple, you can skip to step 5. If you want an intermediate checkpoint, use Rust's format strings:
215	
216	```rust
217	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
218	    let output = format!(
219	        "{header}\n{todos}",
220	        header = result.message.unwrap_or_default(),
221	        todos = result.todos.iter().enumerate()
222	            .map(|(i, t)| format!("{}. [{}] {}", i + 1, t.status, t.title))
223	            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
224	            .join("\n")
225	    );
226	    println!("{}", output);
227	}
228	```
229	
230	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should still work.
231	
232	## 5. Use a MiniJinja Template String
233	
234	Rewrite your `std::fmt` or imperative prints into a MiniJinja template string, and add minijinja to your crate. If you're not familiar with it, it's a Rust implementation of Jinja, pretty much a de-facto standard for more complex templates.
235	
236	**Resources:**
237	
238	- [MiniJinja docs](https://docs.rs/minijinja)
239	- [Jinja syntax reference](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.1.x/templates/)
240	
241	Add minijinja to your `Cargo.toml`:
242	
243	```toml
244	[dependencies]
245	minijinja = "2"
246	```
247	
248	> **A note on booleans and none:** a bare `minijinja::Environment` renders these
249	> the Jinja2 way — `True`, `False`, `None` — from minijinja 2.22 onward.
250	> Standout renders `true`, `false`, and `none`, and normalizes for you from step
251	> 7 on, once rendering goes through `App`. Until then the spelling is
252	> minijinja's. If you want standout's spelling now, add `standout-render = "9"`
253	> next to minijinja and build the environment with
254	> `standout_render::template::new_environment()` instead of
255	> `minijinja::Environment::new()` in the snippets below — the snippets keep the
256	> bare constructor, since `standout` only arrives in step 7.
257	
258	And then you call render in MiniJinja, passing the template string and the data to use. So now your rendering function looks like this:
259	
260	```rust
261	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
262	    let output_tmpl = r#"
263	{% if message %}
264	    {{ message }}
265	{% endif %}
266	{% for todo in todos %}
267	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
268	{% endfor %}
269	"#;
270	
271	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
272	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(output_tmpl).unwrap();
273	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
274	    println!("{}", output);
275	}
276	```
277	
278	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should match (formatting may differ slightly).
279	
280	## 6. Use a Dedicated Template File
281	
282	Now, move the template content into a file (say `src/templates/list.jinja`), and load it in the rendering module. Dedicated files have several advantages: triggering editor/IDE support for the file type, more descriptive diffs, less risk of breaking the code/build and, in the event that you have less technical people helping out with the UI, a much cleaner and simpler way for them to contribute.
283	
284	Create `src/templates/list.jinja`:
285	
286	```jinja
287	{% if message %}{{ message }} {% endif %}
288	{% for todo in todos %}
289	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
290	{% endfor %}
291	```
292	
293	Update your render function to load from file:
294	
295	```rust
296	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
297	    let template_content = include_str!("templates/list.jinja");
298	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
299	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(template_content).unwrap();
300	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
301	    println!("{}", output);
302	}
303	```
304	
305	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should be identical.
306	
307	### Intermezzo B: Declarative Output Definition
308	
309	**What you achieved:** Output is now defined declaratively in a template file, separate from Rust code.
310	**What's now possible:**
311	
312	- Edit templates without recompiling (with minor changes to loading)
313	- Non-Rust developers can contribute to UI
314	- Clear separation in code reviews: "is this a logic change or display change?"
315	- Use partials, filters, and macros for complex outputs (see [Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md))
316	
317	**What's next:** Hooking up Standout for automatic dispatch and rich output.
318	Also, notice we've yet to do anything Standout-specific. This is not a coincidence—the framework is designed around this pattern, making testability, fast iteration, and rich features natural outcomes of the architecture.
319	**Your files now:**
320	
321	```text
322	src/
323	├── main.rs
324	├── handlers.rs
325	├── render.rs
326	└── templates/
327	    └── list.jinja
328	```
329	
330	## 7. Standout: Offload the Handler Orchestration
331	
332	And now the Standout-specific bits finally show up.
333	
334	### 7.1 Add Standout to your Cargo.toml
335	
336	```toml
337	[dependencies]
338	standout = "9"
339	anyhow = "1"
340	```
341	
342	A single `standout` dependency is enough: `standout` re-exports `standout-dispatch`
343	as `standout::dispatch`, and code generated by `#[handler]`, `Questionnaire`, and
344	`QuestionnaireChoices` resolves against whichever of the two crates your
345	`Cargo.toml` declares.
346	
347	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - dependencies should download and compile.
348	
349	### 7.2 Create Handlers with the `#[handler]` Macro
350	
351	The `#[handler]` macro transforms typed Rust functions into Standout-compatible
352	handlers. Keep application behavior in the CLI-free core; the handler annotates
353	CLI parameters, calls the core, and maps its result into serializable view data.
354	
355	See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for full handler API details.
356	
357	```rust
358	use standout::cli::Output;
359	use standout::handler;
360	
361	mod handlers {
362	    use super::*;
363	
364	    // Thin CLI adapter - easy to test, no extraction boilerplate
365	    #[handler]
366	    pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
367	        let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
368	        let todos = core::list(filter)?;
369	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
370	    }
371	
372	    #[handler]
373	    pub fn add(#[arg] title: String) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
374	        let todo = core::add(title)?;
375	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
376	            message: Some(format!("Added: {}", todo.title)),
377	            todos: vec![todo],
378	        }))
379	    }
380	}
381	```
382	
383	The `#[handler]` macro:
384	
385	- Extracts CLI arguments automatically from `ArgMatches`
386	- Converts `#[flag]` to `bool` flags, `#[arg]` to required/optional args
387	- Auto-wraps `Result<T, E>` in `Output::Render` for you
388	
389	**Parameter Annotations:**
390	
391	| Annotation | Type | What it extracts |
392	| ------------ | ------ | ------------------ |
393	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | Boolean flag (`--verbose`) |
394	| `#[arg]` | `T` | Required argument |
395	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | Optional argument |
396	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | Multiple values |
397	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | Access to context (when needed) |
398	
399	### 7.2.1 Connect Commands to Handlers
400	
401	```rust
402	use clap::Subcommand;
403	use standout::cli::Dispatch;
404	
405	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
406	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
407	pub enum Commands {
408	    #[dispatch(pure)]
409	    List {
410	        #[arg(short, long)]
411	        all: bool,
412	    },
413	    #[dispatch(pure)]
414	    Add {
415	        title: String,
416	    },
417	}
418	```
419	
420	The derive macro matches each variant to a handler function by its kebab-case
421	command name (`List` registers as `list`). With `#[dispatch(pure)]`, the
422	variant resolves to the wrapper `#[handler]` generated for the function —
423	`List` → `handlers::list__handler`. Without `pure`, the variant calls
424	`handlers::list` directly, and that function must already have the
425	`fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>` dispatch signature.
426	
427	The `Dispatch` derive connects a variant to a handler; it does not declare the
428	variant's arguments. Those stay clap's, so each variant keeps the fields its
429	handler's `#[flag]` and `#[arg]` parameters read — `all` for `list`, `title`
430	for `add` — exactly as in the plain-clap version at the top of this guide.
431	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports a handler asking for an argument the
432	variant does not declare, which otherwise surfaces as a `get_flag` panic at
433	run time.
434	
435	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
436	
437	### 7.2.2 Accessing App State (Optional)
438	
439	When your handler needs shared resources like databases, use the `#[ctx]` annotation:
440	
441	```rust
442	#[handler]
443	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
444	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
445	    let todos = db.list()?;
446	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
447	}
448	```
449	
450	> **Note:** For the full handler signature (without macros) and advanced patterns, see [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md).
451	
452	### 7.3 Configure AppBuilder
453	
454	Use AppBuilder to configure your app. Instantiate the builder, add the path for your templates. See [App Configuration](../topics/app-configuration.md) for all configuration options.
455	
456	```rust
457	use standout::cli::App;
458	use standout::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
459	
460	let app = App::builder()
461	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))   // Embeds all .jinja/.j2 files
462	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?         // Register handlers from derive macro
463	    .build()?;
464	```
465	
466	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
467	
468	### 7.3.1 Injecting Shared State (Optional)
469	
470	If your handlers need access to shared resources like database connections or configuration, use `app_state`:
471	
472	```rust
473	let app = App::builder()
474	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)    // Shared across all handlers
475	    .app_state(Config::load()?)
476	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
477	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
478	    .build()?;
479	```
480	
481	Handlers retrieve app state via `#[ctx]`:
482	
483	```rust
484	#[handler]
485	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
486	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
487	    let todos = db.list()?;
488	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
489	}
490	```
491	
492	> **Note:** For per-request state (user sessions, request IDs), use pre-dispatch hooks with `ctx.extensions`. See [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) for the full story.
493	
494	### 7.4 Wire up main()
495	
496	The final bit: handling the dispatching off to Standout:
497	
498	```rust
499	use standout::cli::App;
500	use standout::embed_templates;
501	
502	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
503	    let app = App::builder()
504	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
505	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
506	        .build()?;
507	
508	    // Run with auto dispatch - handles parsing and execution
509	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
510	    Ok(())
511	}
512	```
513	
514	If your app has other clap commands that are not managed by Standout, check for unhandled commands. See [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for details on incremental migration.
515	
516	```rust
517	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
518	    // Standout didn't handle this command, fall back to legacy.
519	    legacy_dispatch();
520	}
521	```
522	
523	If the fallback needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`, call `run_with` with a
524	detected target and input sources, then match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`
525	on `into_outcome()`:
526	
527	```rust
528	let target = standout::TargetProperties::detect();
529	let sources = standout::InputSources::from_process();
530	let result = app.run_with(Cli::command(), std::env::args(), target, sources);
531	match result.into_outcome() {
532	    standout::cli::DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches) => legacy_dispatch(matches),
533	    _ => {}
534	}
535	```
536	
537	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - it should work as before.
538	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list --output json` - you should get JSON output for free!
539	
540	And now you can remove the boilerplate: the orchestrator (`list_command`) and
541	the rendering (`render_list`). A single derive attribute links each CLI handler
542	adapter to a command name, a few lines configure Standout, and auto dispatch
543	handles the shell boilerplate.
544	
545	For the next commands you migrate, add a thin adapter plus its template. By
546	default the macro matches the command's name to handlers and template files,
547	but you can map either explicitly.
548	
549	### Intermezzo C: Welcome to Standout
550	
551	**What you achieved:** Full dispatch pipeline with zero boilerplate.
552	
553	**What's now possible:**
554	
555	- Alter the template and re-run your CLI, without compilation, and the new template will be used
556	- Your CLI just got multiple output modes via `--output` (see [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md)):
557	  - **term**: rich shell formatting (more about this on the next step)
558	  - **term-debug**: print formatting info for testing/debugging
559	  - **text**: plain text, no styling
560	  - **auto**: the default, rich term that degrades gracefully
561	  - **json, csv, yaml**: automatic serialization of your data
562	- Pipe output to external commands (jq, clipboard, tee) via `pipe_through`, `pipe_to`, or `pipe_to_clipboard`
563	
564	**What's next:** Adding rich styling to make the output beautiful.
565	
566	**Your files now:**
567	
568	```text
569	src/
570	├── main.rs              # App::builder() setup
571	├── commands.rs          # Commands enum with #[derive(Dispatch)]
572	├── handlers.rs          # list(), add() with #[handler] - CLI adapters returning view data
573	└── templates/
574	    ├── list.jinja
575	    └── add.jinja
576	```
577	
578	## 8. Make the Output Awesome
579	
580	Let's transform that mono-typed, monochrome string into a richer and more useful UI. Borrowing from web apps setup, we keep the content in a template file, and we define styles in a stylesheet file.
581	
582	See [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) for full styling documentation.
583	
584	### 8.1 Create the stylesheet
585	
586	Create `src/styles/default.css`:
587	
588	```css
589	/* Styles for completed todos */
590	.done {
591	    text-decoration: line-through;
592	    color: gray;
593	}
594	
595	/* Style for todo index numbers */
596	.index {
597	    color: yellow;
598	}
599	
600	/* Style for pending todos */
601	.pending {
602	    font-weight: bold;
603	    color: white;
604	}
605	
606	/* Adaptive style for messages */
607	.message {
608	    color: cyan;
609	}
610	
611	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
612	    .pending { color: black; }
613	}
614	
615	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
616	    .pending { color: white; }
617	}
618	```
619	
620	> **Verify:** The file exists at `src/styles/default.css`.
621	
622	### 8.2 Add style tags to your template
623	
624	Update `src/templates/list.jinja` with style tags:
625	
626	```jinja
627	{% if message %}[message]{{ message }}[/message]
628	{% endif %}
629	{% for todo in todos %}
630	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
631	{% endfor %}
632	```
633	
634	The style tags use BBCode-like syntax: `[style-name]content[/style-name]`
635	
636	Notice how we use `[{{ todo.status }}]` dynamically - if `todo.status` is "done", it applies the `.done` style; if it's "pending", it applies the `.pending` style.
637	
638	> **Verify:** The template file is updated.
639	
640	### 8.3 Wire up styles in AppBuilder
641	
642	Add the styles to your app builder:
643	
644	```rust
645	let app = App::builder()
646	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
647	    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))       // Load stylesheets
648	    .default_theme("default")                  // Use styles/default.css
649	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
650	    .build()?;
651	```
652	
653	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
654	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - you should see colored, styled output!
655	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list --output text` - plain text, no colors.
656	
657	Now you're leveraging the core rendering design of Standout:
658	
659	- File-based templates for content, and stylesheets for styles
660	- Custom template syntax with BBCode for markup styles `[style][/style]`
661	- Live reload: iterate through content and styling without recompiling
662	
663	### Intermezzo D: The Full Setup Is Done
664	
665	**What you achieved:** A fully styled, testable, multi-format CLI.
666	
667	**What's now possible:**
668	
669	- Rich terminal output with colors, bold, strikethrough
670	- Automatic light/dark mode adaptation
671	- JSON/YAML/CSV output for scripting and testing
672	- Hot reload of templates and styles during development
673	- Directly testable handler adapters
674	
675	**Your final files:**
676	
677	```text
678	src/
679	├── main.rs              # App::builder() setup
680	├── commands.rs          # Commands enum with #[derive(Dispatch)]
681	├── handlers.rs          # list(), add() with #[handler] - CLI adapters
682	├── templates/
683	│   ├── list.jinja       # with [style] tags
684	│   └── add.jinja
685	└── styles/
686	    └── default.css
687	```
688	
689	For brevity's sake, we've ignored a bunch of finer and relevant points:
690	
691	- The derive macros can set name mapping explicitly: `#[dispatch(handler = custom_fn, template_name = "custom")]`
692	- There are pre-dispatch, post-dispatch and post-render hooks (see [Execution Model](../crates/dispatch/topics/execution-model.md))
693	- Output piping to external commands like `jq`, `tee`, or clipboard (see below and [Output Piping](../crates/pipe/topics/piping.md))
694	- Standout exposes its primitives as standalone crates (see [standout-render](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-rendering.md), [standout-dispatch](../crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md))
695	- Powerful tabular layouts via the `col` filter (see [Tabular Layout](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md))
696	- A help topics system for rich documentation (see [Topics System](../topics/topics-system.md))
697	
698	## Bonus: Pipe Output to External Commands
699	
700	Need to filter output through `jq`, log to a file with `tee`, or copy to clipboard? Standout supports piping rendered output to external commands:
701	
702	```rust
703	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
704	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
705	pub enum Commands {
706	    /// List todos, extracting just titles with jq
707	    #[dispatch(pipe_through = "jq '.todos[].title'")]
708	    List,
709	
710	    /// Export todos to clipboard
711	    #[dispatch(pipe_to_clipboard)]
712	    Export,
713	}
714	```
715	
716	Or via the builder API. `#[handler]` generates a unit struct named after the
717	function with a capitalized suffix (`list` → `list_Handler`) that implements
718	`Handler` directly; register that struct — the plain `handlers::list` function
719	is not itself registrable — with `command_with`:
720	
721	```rust
722	let app = App::builder()
723	    .command_with("list", handlers::list_Handler, |cfg| {
724	        cfg.template_name("list")
725	           .pipe_through("jq '.todos'")  // Filter JSON output
726	    })?
727	    .command_with("export", handlers::export_Handler, |cfg| {
728	        cfg.template_name("export")
729	           .pipe_to("tee /tmp/export.log")  // Log while displaying
730	           .pipe_to_clipboard()  // Then copy to clipboard
731	    })?
732	    .build()?;
733	```
734	
735	Three piping modes:
736	
737	- `pipe_through("cmd")`: Use command's stdout as new output (filters like jq, sort)
738	- `pipe_to("cmd")`: Run command but keep original output (side effects like tee)
739	- `pipe_to_clipboard()`: Send to system clipboard (pbcopy on macOS, xclip on Linux)
740	
741	See [Output Piping](../crates/pipe/topics/piping.md) for the full API.
742	
743	## Bonus: Declarative Input Collection
744	
745	Need to accept input from CLI arguments, piped stdin, environment variables, or interactive prompts? `standout-input` provides declarative input chains, and the `App` builder integrates them as a first-class part of command configuration:
746	
747	```rust
748	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContextInput, FnHandler, Output};
749	use standout::input::{ArgSource, EditorSource, EnvSource, InputChain, StdinSource};
750	
751	App::builder()
752	    .command_with("create", FnHandler::new(create), |cfg| {
753	        cfg.template_name("create")
754	            .input("body", InputChain::<String>::new()
755	                .try_source(ArgSource::new("body"))           // 1. --body argument
756	                .try_source(StdinSource::new())                // 2. Piped stdin
757	                .try_source(EnvSource::new("PR_BODY"))         // 3. Environment variable
758	                .try_source(EditorSource::new().extension(".md"))  // 4. Open editor
759	                .validate(|s| !s.is_empty(), "Body cannot be empty"))
760	    })?
761	    .build()?;
762	
763	fn create(_m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Value> {
764	    // The chain has already been resolved before the handler runs.
765	    let body: &String = ctx.input("body")?;
766	    /* business logic ... */
767	}
768	```
769	
770	Features:
771	
772	- **Declarative priority**: Source order is explicit in the chain
773	- **Framework-integrated**: `.input(name, chain)` registers the chain alongside `template`, `hooks`, and `pipe_*`; resolution happens in pre-dispatch
774	- **Testable**: All sources accept mocks for CI-safe testing (the `TestHarness` from `standout-test` wires them automatically)
775	- **Validated**: Chain-level validation with retry support for interactive sources
776	- **Feature-gated**: Control dependencies (editor, prompts, inquire TUI)
777	
778	The chain still works standalone via `chain.resolve(&matches)?` for cases where input shape depends on already-resolved values.
779	
780	See [Introduction to Input](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) and [Framework Integration](../crates/input/topics/framework-integration.md) for the full guide.
781	
782	Aside from exposing the library primitives, Standout leverages best-in-breed crates like MiniJinja and console::Style under the hood. The lock-in is really negligible: you can use Standout's BB parser or swap it, manually dispatch handlers, and use the renderers directly in your clap dispatch.
783	
784	## Mutable Handlers
785	
786	A closure passed to `command_with` runs as `FnMut`, so it can capture and
787	mutate state directly — no `Arc<Mutex<_>>` wrappers needed. This is common
788	with database connections, file caches, or in-memory indices. Wrap the
789	closure in `FnHandler::new` so it implements `Handler`:
790	
791	```rust
792	use std::collections::HashMap;
793	
794	use clap::ArgMatches;
795	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, FnHandler, Output};
796	use standout::embed_templates;
797	use uuid::Uuid;
798	
799	struct PadStore {
800	    index: HashMap<Uuid, Metadata>,
801	}
802	
803	impl PadStore {
804	    fn complete(&mut self, id: Uuid) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
805	        // This needs &mut self
806	        self.index.get_mut(&id).unwrap().completed = true;
807	        Ok(())
808	    }
809	}
810	
811	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
812	    let mut store = PadStore::load()?;
813	
814	    App::builder()
815	        .app_state(Config::load()?)
816	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
817	        .command_with(
818	            "complete",
819	            FnHandler::new(|m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
820	                let id = m.get_one::<Uuid>("id").unwrap();
821	                store.complete(*id)?; // &mut store works!
822	                Ok(Output::Silent)
823	            }),
824	            |cfg| cfg.silent(),
825	        )?
826	        .command_with(
827	            "list",
828	            FnHandler::new(|_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
829	                Ok(Output::Render(store.list()))
830	            }),
831	            |cfg| cfg,
832	        )?
833	        .build()?
834	        .run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
835	    Ok(())
836	}
837	```
838	
839	**Handler capabilities:**
840	
841	- `command_with` accepts anything implementing `Handler`; `FnHandler::new`
842	  turns a plain `FnMut` closure into one
843	- Handlers can capture `&mut` references to state
844	- The `Handler` trait uses `&mut self` for struct-based handlers
845	- No `Send + Sync` requirements—CLI apps are single-threaded
846	
847	## Appendix: Common Errors and Troubleshooting
848	
849	- Template not found
850	  - **Error:** `template 'list' not found`
851	  - **Cause:** The template path in `embed_templates!` doesn't match your file structure.
852	  - **Fix:** Ensure the path is relative to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g., `embed_templates!("src/templates")` and that the file is named `list.jinja`, `list.j2`, or `list.txt`.
853	- Style not applied
854	  - **Symptom:** Text appears but without colors/formatting.
855	  - **Cause:** Style name in template doesn't match stylesheet.
856	  - **Fix:** Check that `[mystyle]` in your template matches `.mystyle` in CSS or `mystyle:` in YAML. Run with `--output term-debug` to see style tag names.
857	- Handler not called
858	  - **Symptom:** Command runs but nothing happens or wrong handler runs.
859	  - **Cause:** Command name mismatch between clap enum variant and handler function.
860	  - **Fix:** Ensure enum variant `List` maps to function `handlers::list` (snake_case conversion). Or use explicit mapping: `#[dispatch(handler = my_custom_handler)]`
861	- JSON output is empty or wrong
862	  - **Symptom:** `--output json` produces unexpected results.
863	  - **Cause:** `Serialize` derive is missing or field names don't match template expectations.
864	  - **Fix:** Ensure all types in your result implement `Serialize`. Use `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` for consistent naming.
865	- Styles not loading
866	  - **Error:** `theme not found: default`
867	  - **Cause:** Stylesheet file missing or wrong path.
868	  - **Fix:** Ensure `src/styles/default.css` exists. Check `embed_styles!` path matches your file structure.
869

# Upgrading from Standout 5.0.0 to 6.0.0

This is a minor upgrade. Only one internal change landed, and it is transparent for most users.

## Quick Summary

| Version   | What Changed                                                           |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **6.0.0** | Internal dispatch fix: theme resolved at runtime instead of build time |

## Step 1: Update Cargo.toml

```diff
[dependencies]
- standout = "5"
+ standout = "6"
```

## Step 2: Check for custom DispatchFn (unlikely)

This only affects you if you wrote custom dispatch functions using the internal `DispatchFn` type directly. The signature changed to accept `&Theme` at runtime:

```diff
- type DispatchFn = Box<dyn Fn(ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> RunResult>;
+ type DispatchFn = Box<dyn Fn(ArgMatches, &CommandContext, &Theme) -> RunResult>;
```

If you only use the public API (`.command()`, `.commands()`, `#[derive(Dispatch)]`), **no code changes are needed**. The benefit is that `.theme()` and `.commands()` can now be called in any order without the theme being silently ignored.

## That's It

If you weren't using internal dispatch types, upgrading is just a version bump. All public APIs are unchanged.

Standout has since moved past 6.0.0; check the current API against the crate you depend on rather than treating this guide as a description of today's surface.
4

6	
7	| Version | What Changed |
8	| --------- | ------------- |
9	| **4.0.0** | `App`/`LocalApp` unified into single-threaded `App` |
10	| **5.0.0** | New `standout-input` crate (additive, no breakage) |
11	| **6.0.0** | Internal dispatch fix for theme ordering (transparent for most users) |
12	
13	The only version that requires code changes for most users is **4.0.0**.
14	
15	## Step 1: Update Cargo.toml
16	
17	```diff
18	[dependencies]
19	- standout = "3.8"
20	+ standout = "6"
21	```
22	
23	## Step 2: Remove LocalApp / ThreadSafe / Local types (v4.0.0)
24	
25	The dual `App`/`LocalApp` architecture has been removed. CLI apps are single-threaded, so the thread-safety distinction was unnecessary.
26	
27	### Removed types
28	
29	These types no longer exist:
30	
31	- `LocalApp`, `LocalAppBuilder`
32	- `LocalHandler`
33	- `Local`, `ThreadSafe` marker types
34	- `HandlerMode` trait

36	### Update imports

38	```diff
39	- use standout::cli::{App, ThreadSafe, LocalApp, LocalHandler};
40	+ use standout::cli::{App, Handler};
41	```
42	
43	### Update App::builder() calls
44	
45	`App::builder()` no longer takes a generic type parameter:
46	
47	```diff
48	- App::<ThreadSafe>::builder()
49	+ App::builder()
50	      .command("list", handler, template)?
51	      .build()?
52	```
53	
54	If you were using `LocalApp`:
55	
56	```diff
57	- LocalApp::builder()
58	+ App::builder()
59	      .command("list", handler, template)?
60	      .build()?
61	```
62	
63	### Update Handler implementations
64	
65	`Handler::handle()` now takes `&mut self` instead of `&self`:
66	
67	```diff
68	  impl Handler for MyHandler {
69	-     fn handle(&self, m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
70	+     fn handle(&mut self, m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
71	          // ...
72	      }
73	  }
74	```

93	- let state: Arc<Extensions> = ctx.app_state.clone();
94	+ use std::rc::Rc;
95	+ let state: Rc<Extensions> = ctx.app_state.clone();

98	`Arc` has been replaced with `Rc` throughout since thread-safety is no longer needed.

103

107	```
108	
109	If you only use the public API (`.command()`, `.commands()`, `#[derive(Dispatch)]`), this change is transparent. The benefit is that `.theme()` and `.commands()` can now be called in any order.

# Upgrading from Standout 3.8.0 to 6.0.0

Standout went through three major version bumps since 3.8.0 (4.0, 5.0, 6.0). This guide covers everything you need to change to get your code compiling and working on 6.0.0. Standout has since moved past 6.0.0; check the current API against the crate you depend on rather than treating this guide as a description of today's surface.

## Quick Summary

| Version | What Changed |
| --------- | ------------- |
| **4.0.0** | `App`/`LocalApp` unified into single-threaded `App` |
| **5.0.0** | New `standout-input` crate (additive, no breakage) |
| **6.0.0** | Internal dispatch fix for theme ordering (transparent for most users) |

The only version that requires code changes for most users is **4.0.0**.

## Step 1: Update Cargo.toml

```diff
[dependencies]
- standout = "3.8"
+ standout = "6"
```

## Step 2: Remove LocalApp / ThreadSafe / Local types (v4.0.0)

The dual `App`/`LocalApp` architecture has been removed. CLI apps are single-threaded, so the thread-safety distinction was unnecessary.

### Removed types

These types no longer exist:

- `LocalApp`, `LocalAppBuilder`
- `LocalHandler`
- `Local`, `ThreadSafe` marker types
- `HandlerMode` trait

### Update imports

```diff
- use standout::cli::{App, ThreadSafe, LocalApp, LocalHandler};
+ use standout::cli::{App, Handler};
```

### Update App::builder() calls

`App::builder()` no longer takes a generic type parameter:

```diff
- App::<ThreadSafe>::builder()
+ App::builder()
      .command("list", handler, template)?
      .build()?
```

If you were using `LocalApp`:

```diff
- LocalApp::builder()
+ App::builder()
      .command("list", handler, template)?
      .build()?
```

### Update Handler implementations

`Handler::handle()` now takes `&mut self` instead of `&self`:

```diff
  impl Handler for MyHandler {
-     fn handle(&self, m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
+     fn handle(&mut self, m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
          // ...
      }
  }
```

This means you can mutate handler state directly, without `Arc<Mutex<_>>` wrappers.

### Update closure handlers

Handler closures are now `FnMut` instead of `Fn`:

```diff
- let handler: Box<dyn Fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>> = ...;
+ let handler: Box<dyn FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>> = ...;
```

In practice, most closures work without changes. The difference matters only if you were explicitly annotating types.

### Update CommandContext.app_state references

```diff
- use std::sync::Arc;
- let state: Arc<Extensions> = ctx.app_state.clone();
+ use std::rc::Rc;
+ let state: Rc<Extensions> = ctx.app_state.clone();
```

`Arc` has been replaced with `Rc` throughout since thread-safety is no longer needed.

## Step 3: Check for custom DispatchFn (v6.0.0)

This only affects you if you wrote custom dispatch functions using the internal `DispatchFn` type. The signature changed to accept `&Theme` at runtime:

```diff
- type DispatchFn = Box<dyn Fn(ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> RunResult>;
+ type DispatchFn = Box<dyn Fn(ArgMatches, &CommandContext, &Theme) -> RunResult>;
```

If you only use the public API (`.command()`, `.commands()`, `#[derive(Dispatch)]`), this change is transparent. The benefit is that `.theme()` and `.commands()` can now be called in any order.

## Common Compiler Errors and Fixes

### `cannot find type LocalApp in module cli`

Replace `LocalApp` with `App`. See Step 2.

### `cannot find type ThreadSafe`

Remove the type parameter from `App::<ThreadSafe>::builder()`. See Step 2.

### `method handle has an incompatible type for trait`

Change `&self` to `&mut self` in your `Handler` impl. See Step 2.

### `expected Rc, found Arc`

Replace `Arc` with `Rc` for `app_state` references. See Step 2.

## New Features Available After Upgrading

These are additive and don't require changes, but you may want to take advantage of them:

### standout-input (v5.0.0)

Declarative input collection from multiple sources with fallback chains:

```rust
use standout_input::{InputChain, ArgSource, StdinSource, EditorSource};

let message = InputChain::<String>::new()
    .try_source(ArgSource::new("message"))
    .try_source(StdinSource::new())
    .try_source(EditorSource::new())
    .resolve(&matches)?;
```

Sources include: CLI args, stdin, environment variables, clipboard, editor, and interactive prompts. See [Introduction to Input](../../crates/standout-input/docs/guides/intro-to-input.md) for the full guide.

### #[handler] macro (v3.6.1)

If you're still writing handlers with manual `ArgMatches` extraction, the `#[handler]` macro eliminates boilerplate:

```rust
// Before
fn list(m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let all = m.get_flag("all");
    let items = storage::list(all)?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}

// After
#[handler]
fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Vec<Item>, Error> {
    storage::list(all)
}
```

### Auto-wrap `Result<T>` (v3.6.1)

Handlers can return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `Ok(Output::Render(...))`:

```rust
fn list(m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Vec<Item>, Error> {
    storage::list()  // no more Ok(Output::Render(...)) wrapping
}
```

### Output piping (v3.6.1)

Pipe handler output to external commands or the clipboard:

```rust
App::builder()
    .commands(|g| {
        g.command_with("list", handlers::list, |cfg| {
            cfg.template("list.jinja")
               .pipe_through("jq '.data'")
        })
    })
```

#!/bin/zsh
# Acceptance probe for SPEC.md. Run from the app directory.
B=./target/debug/validity
mkdir -p .probe
OUT=.probe/out; ERR=.probe/err
pass=0; fail=0

# run <expected_exit> <label> -- <args...>
check() {
  local want=$1; shift
  local label=$1; shift
  "$B" "$@" >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"
  local st=$?
  local ok=1
  [[ $st == $want ]] || { ok=0; echo "FAIL[$label]: exit $st want $want"; }
  echo "$label|exit=$st|out=$(wc -c <"$OUT"|tr -d ' ')B|err=$(wc -c <"$ERR"|tr -d ' ')B"
  (( ok )) && (( pass++ )) || (( fail++ ))
}

has_ansi() { LC_ALL=C grep -q $'\x1b\[' "$1"; }
markers='\[(about|header|usage|item|metavar|desc|default|values|example)\?\]'

echo "== success bytes =="
for a in "show ok" "early" "late" "nest inner leaf"; do
  "$B" ${=a} --output text >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"; st=$?
  b=$(xxd -p <"$OUT")
  [[ "$b" == "6f6b0a" && $st == 0 && ! -s "$ERR" ]] \
    && { echo "ok  $a --output text -> 'ok\\n'"; (( pass++ )) } \
    || { echo "FAIL $a --output text -> $b exit=$st stderr=$(cat $ERR)"; (( fail++ )) }
  # piped, no --output
  "$B" ${=a} >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"; st=$?
  b=$(xxd -p <"$OUT")
  [[ "$b" == "6f6b0a" && $st == 0 ]] \
    && { echo "ok  $a (piped) -> 'ok\\n'"; (( pass++ )) } \
    || { echo "FAIL $a (piped) -> $b exit=$st"; (( fail++ )) }
done

echo "== term mode with color forced =="
for a in "show ok" "early" "late" "nest inner leaf"; do
  CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 "$B" ${=a} --output term >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"; st=$?
  txt=$(LC_ALL=C sed $'s/\x1b\\[[0-9;]*m//g' "$OUT")
  if [[ $st == 0 && "$txt" == "ok" ]] && has_ansi "$OUT" && ! grep -Eq "$markers" "$OUT"; then
    echo "ok  $a --output term (forced color): styled, visible 'ok'"; (( pass++ ))
  else
    echo "FAIL $a --output term: exit=$st text='$txt' ansi=$(has_ansi "$OUT" && echo yes || echo no)"; (( fail++ ))
  fi
done

echo "== failure cases =="
for n in okk nosuch; do
  for mode in "" "--output text" "--output term"; do
    "$B" show $n ${=mode} >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"; st=$?
    if [[ $st == 1 && ! -s "$OUT" ]] && grep -q "$n" "$ERR" \
       && ! grep -qF '{{' "$ERR" && ! grep -qF '{%' "$ERR"; then
      echo "ok  show $n $mode -> exit 1, empty stdout, stderr names '$n'"; (( pass++ ))
    else
      echo "FAIL show $n $mode -> exit=$st stdout='$(cat $OUT)' stderr='$(cat $ERR)'"; (( fail++ ))
    fi
  done
done

echo "== help =="
help_case() {
  local label="$1"; shift
  local forced="$1"; shift
  if [[ $forced == force ]]; then
    CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 "$B" "$@" >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"
  else
    "$B" "$@" >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"
  fi
  local st=$?
  local problems=()
  [[ $st == 0 ]] || problems+=("exit=$st")
  [[ -s "$OUT" ]] || problems+=("empty stdout")
  [[ -s "$ERR" ]] && problems+=("stderr: $(cat $ERR)")
  grep -Eq "$markers" "$OUT" && problems+=("unresolved marker")
  grep -qi "usage" "$OUT" || problems+=("no usage line")
  if (( ${#problems} == 0 )); then echo "ok  $label"; (( pass++ ))
  else echo "FAIL $label: ${problems[*]}"; (( fail++ )); fi
}

help_case "help --output text" plain help --output text
help_case "help --output term" plain help --output term
help_case "help (forced color, term)" force help --output term
help_case "--help" plain --help
help_case "-h" plain -h
help_case "leaf --help" plain nest inner leaf --help
help_case "leaf -h" plain nest inner leaf -h
help_case "leaf help" plain nest inner leaf help

echo "== help content =="
"$B" help --output text >"$OUT" 2>&1
for w in show early late nest; do
  grep -q "\b$w\b" "$OUT" && { echo "ok  root help names $w"; (( pass++ )) } || { echo "FAIL root help missing $w"; (( fail++ )) }
done
"$B" nest inner leaf --help >"$OUT" 2>&1
grep -q "leaf" "$OUT" && { echo "ok  leaf help names leaf"; (( pass++ )) } || { echo "FAIL leaf help missing leaf"; (( fail++ )) }

echo "== help ansi =="
CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 "$B" help --output term >"$OUT" 2>&1
has_ansi "$OUT" && { echo "ok  help --output term (forced) carries ANSI"; (( pass++ )) } || { echo "FAIL help term carries no ANSI"; (( fail++ )) }
"$B" help --output text >"$OUT" 2>&1
has_ansi "$OUT" && { echo "FAIL help --output text carries ANSI"; (( fail++ )) } || { echo "ok  help --output text has no ANSI"; (( pass++ )) }
NO_COLOR=1 CLICOLOR=0 "$B" help --output term >"$OUT" 2>&1
has_ansi "$OUT" && { echo "FAIL help term with color off carries ANSI"; (( fail++ )) } || { echo "ok  help term with color off has no ANSI"; (( pass++ )) }
"$B" show ok --output text >"$OUT" 2>&1
has_ansi "$OUT" && { echo "FAIL show ok --output text carries ANSI"; (( fail++ )) } || { echo "ok  show ok --output text has no ANSI"; (( pass++ )) }

echo "== usage errors (exit 2) =="
check 2 "nest" nest
check 2 "nest inner" nest inner
check 2 "unknown command" bogus
check 2 "unknown flag" --nope
check 2 "show with no name" show

echo
echo "pass=$pass fail=$fail"

## Auto Mode

`Auto` is the default when `--output` is absent, and an application can change
that default with
[`output_mode_fallback(mode)`](./app-configuration.md#output-mode-fallback) — an
explicit `--output` still outranks it. `Auto` queries the terminal for color
support:

```rust
Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
```

If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).

This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:

```bash
myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
```

## The --output Flag

Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:

```bash
myapp list --output=auto        # Default
myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
```

The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.

## Term vs Text

**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:

```bash
myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
```

Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
into `term`.

**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:

```bash
myapp list --output=text
```

Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.

Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
them itself.

`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
against `term` or `text`.

## TermDebug Mode

TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

#!/bin/zsh
# Acceptance probe for SPEC.md. Run from the app directory.
B=./target/debug/validity
mkdir -p .probe
OUT=.probe/out; ERR=.probe/err
pass=0; fail=0

# run <expected_exit> <label> -- <args...>
check() {
  local want=$1; shift
  local label=$1; shift
  "$B" "$@" >"$OUT" 2>"$ERR"
  local st=$?
  local ok=1
  [[ $st == $want ]] || { ok=0; echo "FAIL[$label]: exit $st want $want"; }
  echo "$label|exit=$st|out=$(wc -c <"$OUT"|tr -d ' ')B|err=$(wc -c <"$ERR"|tr -d ' ')B"

#! standout-answers 1
#! questionnaire: corpus.exit
